kernels.definition: A variable is a name that refers to a stored value; the assignment operator = binds the name on the left to the value produced on the right (for objects it binds the reference, so no copy is made).

definitionAnchor.quote: Variables allow programs to refer to values using names rather than memory locations

facts.text: A statement sets a variable to a value using the assignment operator (=), with the name on the left and the value on the right.

anchor.quote: A statement can set a variable to a value using the assignment operator (=)

facts.text: Assignment is not mathematical equality — = copies a value into a variable rather than asserting two sides are equal.

anchor.quote: Note that this is different from the equal sign of mathematics

facts.text: A variable name may contain letters, digits, and underscores and be any length, but cannot start with a digit.

anchor.quote: A variable name can consist of letters, digits, and underscores and be of any length

facts.text: Variable names are case-sensitive, so total and Total are two different variables.

anchor.quote: Also, letter case matters

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §1.3 Variables

kernels.definition: Every Python value has a data type (such as int, float, or str); expressions combine values, and conversion functions move a value from one type to another.

definitionAnchor.quote: explicit type conversion to convert one data type to another

facts.text: The interpreter performs implicit type conversion to promote types automatically inside a mixed expression.

anchor.quote: The Python interpreter uses implicit type conversion to automatically convert one data type to another

facts.text: int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3.

anchor.quote: int() converts a data type to an integer. Any fractional part is removed

facts.text: True division (/) converts numbers to floats before dividing and always returns a float.

anchor.quote: True division (/) converts numbers to floats before dividing

facts.text: Floor division (//) computes the whole-number quotient, discarding the remainder.

anchor.quote: Floor division (//) computes the quotient, or the number of times divided

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §2.2 Type conversion; §2.5 Dividing integers

kernels.definition: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.

definitionAnchor.quote: When an if-else statement is executed, one and only one of the branches is taken

facts.text: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.

anchor.quote: If the condition is true, the body is executed. If the condition is false, the body is not executed

facts.text: An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.

anchor.quote: An else statement is used with an if statement and contains a body of statements that is executed when the if statement's condition is false

facts.text: and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.

anchor.quote: The and operator takes two condition operands and returns True if both conditions are true

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §4.2 If-else statements; §4.3 Boolean operations

kernels.definition: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.

definitionAnchor.quote: A while loop is a code construct that runs a set of statements, known as the loop body, while a given condition, known as the loop expression, is true

facts.text: After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue.

anchor.quote: At each iteration, once the loop statement is executed, the loop expression is evaluated again

facts.text: If the loop expression is true, the body runs again; if it is false, the loop terminates.

anchor.quote: If true, the loop body will execute at least one more time. If false, the loop's execution will terminate

facts.text: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.

anchor.quote: the loop body must make progress toward ending the condition

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §5.1 While loop

kernels.definition: A for loop iterates over each element of a container — a range of numbers, a string, or a list — binding a loop variable to one element at a time.

definitionAnchor.quote: A for loop iterates over all elements in a container

facts.text: A container can be a range of numbers, a string of characters, or a list of values.

anchor.quote: In Python, a container can be a range of numbers, a string of characters, or a list of values

facts.text: The loop retrieves the objects of a container one at a time.

anchor.quote: an iterative loop can be designed to retrieve objects one at a time

facts.text: range() produces a sequence of integers and is commonly paired with a for loop to repeat the body a fixed number of times; range(n) yields 0 through n-1.

anchor.quote: The range() function produces a sequence of integers

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §5.2 For loop

kernels.definition: A function is a named, reusable block of code defined with def that runs only when it is called; variables created inside it are local to that call.

definitionAnchor.quote: A function is a named, reusable block of code that performs a task when called

facts.text: A function is defined with the def keyword, a name, parentheses, and a colon, with an indented body.

anchor.quote: A function is defined using the def keyword

facts.text: A variable's scope is the part of the program where it can be accessed.

anchor.quote: A variable's scope is the part of a program where the variable can be accessed

facts.text: A variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function.

anchor.quote: A variable created within a function has local scope and only exists within the function

facts.text: A variable created outside any function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.

anchor.quote: A variable created outside of a function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §6.1 Defining functions; §6.3 Variable scope

mcItems.q: In a debug trace, which action matches Python assignment when `total = 7` runs?
op: It binds `total` to the value 7.
It checks whether `total` and 7 are equal.
It creates a new variable named `7`.
It copies 7 into every existing name.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is the binding of the name on the left to the value on the right. The closest distractor is the equality check, but assignment is not mathematical equality; the evidence is the rule that `=` binds a name to a produced value rather than asserting two sides are equal.

mcItems.q: Which pair names two different variables in Python?
op: score and Score
score and score1
score_1 and score1
1score and score
mcItems.ex: `score` and `Score` are different because variable names are case-sensitive. The closest distractor is `score` and `score1`, but that differs by added digits rather than by case; the evidence that rules it out is the claim that case changes alone can make two different variables.

keyTerms.df: A named reference to a stored value; the name points to a value already in memory.
keyTerms.eg: After `total = 7`, `total` refers to the value 7.
keyTerms.mi: A variable is the value itself, not a name.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that the name refers to the stored value, so later code can use the name to access it.

keyTerms.df: A statement that uses `=` to bind a name on the left to the value on the right.
keyTerms.eg: `count = 3` binds `count` to 3.
keyTerms.mi: It means the two sides are mathematically equal.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that `=` in Python performs binding, not an equality test or proof.

mcItems.q: A student evaluates 7 / 2 in Python. Which result matches the evidence?
op: 3.5 as a float
3 as an int
4 as an int
3.0 as a float
mcItems.ex: 7 / 2 uses true division, which converts numbers to floats before dividing and always returns a float. The closest distractor is 3 as an int, but that would require floor division or truncation, not true division.

mcItems.q: A program computes int(8 / 3) after the division step. What value does it produce?
op: 2 as an int
3 as an int
0 as an int
mcItems.ex: 8 / 3 first becomes a float because true division always returns a float, and int() then removes the fractional part. The closest distractor is 2.6666666666666665 as a float, but that would be the division result before int() converts it.

keyTerms.df: Automatic promotion of values inside a mixed expression so the expression can be evaluated.
keyTerms.eg: In a mixed numeric expression, the interpreter can promote types automatically before computing the result.
keyTerms.mi: It means Python changes every value only when a programmer calls a conversion function.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that the interpreter can perform the conversion on its own inside a mixed expression.

keyTerms.df: Division that returns the whole-number quotient and leaves out the remainder.
keyTerms.eg: A division like 7 // 2 gives the quotient without the leftover part.
keyTerms.mi: It always produces a float because all division in Python returns floats.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that true division returns a float, while floor division keeps only the whole-number quotient.

mcItems.q: A debugging print shows `x = 4` and `y = 9`. Which condition makes the `if` body run only when both values are above 5?
op: x > 5 and y > 5
x > 5 or y > 5
not x > 5 and y > 5
x > 5 and not y > 5
mcItems.ex: `and` is the only operator here that is true only when both comparisons are true. The closest distractor is `or`, but that would run the body when just one value is above 5, which is a different state from the one required.

mcItems.q: In a trace, the condition `score > 80` evaluates to false. What happens next in an `if-else` block?
op: The if body runs anyway because the test was checked.
Only the else block runs.
Both blocks run in sequence.
Neither block runs until the next condition.
mcItems.ex: When an `if` condition is false, the `if` body is skipped and the `else` clause runs. The closest misconception is that the `if` body still executes after a false test, but the evidence rules that out because false skips the `if` body.

keyTerms.df: A way to combine truth values into a single test.
keyTerms.eg: A condition like `a > 0 and b > 0` checks two comparisons together before choosing a branch.
keyTerms.mi: It means a variable can only be True or False.
keyTerms.cx: Boolean logic uses operators such as `and`, `or`, and `not` to build compound conditions.

keyTerms.df: A block reserved for the opposite case of a false test.
keyTerms.eg: If `temp > 100` is false, the `else` block can print `safe to continue`.
keyTerms.mi: It is another name for a second `if` statement.
keyTerms.cx: An `else` runs when the `if` condition is false; it does not ask a new question.

mcItems.q: A student is debugging a counter-controlled while loop that prints the value of n, then subtracts 1 from n. The student asks which evidence best shows the loop will stop on the next check.
op: n changes before the condition is checked again.
n is printed once before the body starts.
the same value of n appears in two separate runs.
the loop body contains a print statement.
mcItems.ex: Correct: the decrement changes n before the condition is evaluated again, so the next re-check can turn false. The closest distractor is the repeated print, but repeated output alone does not prove the stopping condition changes; the key evidence is the state change in n.

mcItems.q: A loop keeps running during debugging, and the condition is still true after each pass through the body. Which diagnosis is best supported by that evidence?
op: the loop may be infinite because the body is not making progress toward false.
the loop must already have ended after the first pass.
the condition is being checked only after the loop finishes.
the body cannot run again once the condition is true.
mcItems.ex: Correct: if the condition never becomes false, the loop can run forever, which is an infinite loop. The closest distractor is the claim that the loop has ended after one pass, but the observed evidence says the condition is still true after re-checking, so termination is not supported.

keyTerms.df: A test whose truth value controls whether another pass runs.
keyTerms.eg: In while n > 0:, the test n > 0 decides whether the next iteration happens.
keyTerms.mi: It is the line that changes the variable each time.
keyTerms.cx: The body changes state; the condition is the check that gets re-evaluated before each iteration.

keyTerms.df: A loop that keeps repeating because its test never turns false.
keyTerms.eg: If a counter never decreases, while counter > 0: can continue forever.
keyTerms.mi: Any loop that runs more than once is infinite.
keyTerms.cx: Repeated execution is normal; it becomes infinite only when the condition never becomes false and the body does not move toward ending it.

mcItems.q: What does `for item in range(3):` do to `item` over the loop?
op: Binds `item` to 0, then 1, then 2.
Keeps `item` fixed at 3 for every pass.
Binds `item` to the characters in `3`.

the body cannot run again once the condition is true.
